question: May I connect another players brewery with two new railways and then pickup his beer for the actions costs?
answer: When laying two rail links, each one is considered a separate construction, so the first must connect to coal before the second is built. However, since only one beer is required, it is only the second rail that must have access to beer after being built. (Use normal rules to access beer.)
manual quote 1:
In a single Network action, you may build a maximum of 2 rail Links for £15, if you also consume 1 beer. This beer must be consumed from a Brewery (not a Merchant beer).
Remember: If consuming beer from another player’s Brewery, it must be connected to the second rail Link (after it is placed)
manual quote 2:
You must consume 1 coal for each
rail Link built (see “Consuming Coal”)
Remember: Each rail Link is placed
separately and must be connected to a
source of coal (after it is placed).

question: Since you need coal to build a rail link, and assuming there aren't any existing links on the board, are Coal market adjacent tracks the only place we can build rail links in the Rail Era?
answer: To consume coal, you need to be connected to a market or an unflipped coal mine after it is placed.
manual quote 1: To consume coal, a rail Link or Industry tile must be connected to a source of coal (after it is placed).
manual quote 2: Coal must be consumed from: 1 The closest (fewest Link tiles distant) connected unflipped Coal Mine
manual quote 3: 2 If you are not connected to an unflipped Coal Mine, you can purchase coal from the Coal Market

question: In a 4 player game, there are 64 action cards. Every player puts one card face down beneath his player board, so 60 cards are remaining. Each epoch has 8 rounds, 2 cards are played per player per round. That gives 8*2*4 = 64 required cards. Is it correct?
answer: Yes, the first round of the game has only one action per player, so at the end of first round every player has 2 card in the discard pile. From the 2nd round on every player proceeds with the usual 2 actions.
manual quote 1: Player Area Setup:
manual quote 2:
8- Draw 8 cards from the Draw Deck; this is your Hand. Do not reveal your Hand to other players.
9- Draw 1 additional card from the Draw Deck and place it face down in your player area; this is your Discard Pile.
manual quote 3: There are exactly 8/9/10 rounds per era in a 4/3/2-players game.
manual quote 4:
On your turn, perform a total of 2 actions.
Exception: During the first round of the Canal Era, each player performs only 1 action. 

For each action you perform, you must discard a card from your Hand and place it face up on top of your Discard Pile.

question: When an industry tile is overbuilt, the new industry tile is placed in its unflipped state, regardless of whether the original tile was flipped. Is that correct?
answer: Yes, unflipped state. You've essentially torn down the old factory, built a new on in its place and still need to sell its goods.
manual quote 1: Sometimes you are allowed to replace an already placed Industry tile with a higher-level tile of the same industry type (you must still pay the necessary build costs). This is known as Overbuilding.
manual quote 2: You may Overbuild any of your Industry tiles without restriction.

question: Let's suppose, at one market location, one merchant tile buys manufactures and the other merchant tile buys all of manufacturer, mill and pottery and both have common beer still available. If I am selling manufacturer of my own, can I take the beer from the second merchant tile first where it accepts all of them?
answer: You have a free choice of which beer to use, and in this case I really can't see any reason why you wouldn't grab the all-goods merchant beer.
manual quote 1: To perform the Sell action
manual quote 2: Choose 1 of your unflipped Cotton Mill, Manufacturer, or Pottery tiles, that is connected to a Merchant tile featuring that industry’s icon
manual quote 3: Consume the required amount of beer, shown in the top right corner of the Industry tile. question:
Is our way of playing is correct?
1) Play a card, declare your action, any associated cost instantly goes next to your player marker NOT the card. 
2) Draw a card to fill back up to 8 
3) Play your second card using the same rules as #1 on this example 
4) Instantly redraw back up to 8 
5) Money goes to the bank, then income is done (can be plus or minus depending on income track marker) 
6) Everyone already has 8 cards so no redraw required 
7) Next turn in order of player marker
answer: It is correct except you don’t draw cards until both of your cards are spent so that your turn is over, then you refill your hand up to 8 by drawing 2 (unless the deck is empty).  It’s in the rulebook under “player turns”.

On your turn, perform a total of 2 actions.

manual quote 7: Afterwards, take all money from the Character tiles, and place it back into the Bank

question: Assuming I have no adjacent Link to a location, Can I build a link out of a city from industry tiles not belonging to me?

question: if I built an Industry Tile that requires two coal, and it is equally close to two Coal Mines (assuming both mines have more than 1 coal), can I consume 1 coal each from both mines?

question: If I am connected to location X via a canal /train, but I do not build any industry on this location, am I allowed to place a canal /train on the other side of the empty location? Is it still considered part of my network?

The location is still considered part of your network if you have your link adjacent to it even though it is filled with industry tiles of your opponent. Connected means that you can trace a route to that location with any player 's link. Thus, if the link belong to your opponents you cannot build the link on the other side.

question: How can I logically and thematically explain/understand why we will consume the coal/iron/beer from other players' factories without paying them anything for it?
answer: I wouldn’t say it’s thematic per se, but the game features economic abstractions. Your railways benefit the coal mines of other players. This increases their profits and yours. Exploiting the interdependency of industries is what you are doing, not managing the balance sheet of individual transactions. The details of how much might be paid for actual goods are abstracted into the game. Explicitly, when tiles flip, they don’t stop making money - the ongoing profits are now part of your game income level.

question: What if you have no industries or links on the map?

question: The rules state that "Sometimes you are allowed …" to overbuild. However, I can find nothing in the rules that states what "sometimes" mean?
answer: The rule is you can always overbuild your own industries if the conditions are met. You can overbuild other players' Iron Works or Coal Mines, but only if there are no cubes of the corresponding resource on the board (including in the market). You can never overbuild opponents' other industries.

- There must be no resource cubes on the entire board, including in its Market, of the same type as the Industry tile being replaced.

question: How many networks can you have?
answer: Well, the rules refer to all the locations that either have one of your buildings or one of your links going into them as “your network”, singular. So technically, you really can only have one network but it can consist of unconnected parts.

question: Is this always true that selling one industry is usually an efficiency failure?
answer: With time you'll notice that the most scarce and valuable resource you have are your actions. So it tends to be better to make multiple sales with a single Sell action, and to build two railroad links with a single Network action. All within reason, though. Sniping a free beer from an opponent to block them from making a sale when they're strained for cash is a circumstance worth considering. Depending on the scenario, you're better off closing a sale to flip an industry or industry + brewery tiles so that the added income open up your game in the following rounds.There's no "always true" here. Just a damn strong tendency.
